opus-5.5.text:
I think it's mostly about density. San Francisco has an unusually high concentration of people who have actually trained large models: researchers, engineers, and infrastructure people who have been through the whole cycle of pretraining, post-training, and deployment. If you want to start a new lab, the scarcest resource is that talent, not ideas or even compute, and those people are clustered here. You can have coffee with three or four of them in one afternoon.

Second, the capital is here. Investors in the Bay Area have become very comfortable writing large checks for research-heavy companies that may not have revenue for a while. That's quite unusual. In many other places a founder would have to justify a business model from day one, but here a strong team with a credible technical direction can raise money to buy GPUs and just start.

Third, there's the information flow. The field is moving so fast that a lot of the real knowledge isn't in papers yet. It's in conversations: what worked, what didn't, which scaling tricks are real, which ones are noise. Being physically close to that network gives you a few months' head start, and in this field a few months matters a lot.

There's also a cultural factor. People here are used to the idea that you can leave a big company, start something risky, and if it fails, that's fine. You'll find another good opportunity. That lowers the psychological cost of trying. When I talk to friends who have left big labs to start their own, many say the decision felt natural precisely because so many people around them had done the same thing.

Finally, there's a kind of self-reinforcing loop. Once OpenAI, Anthropic, and others established themselves here, everything else followed: the talent, the startups building on top of them, the infrastructure providers, the events and meetups. Now if you're serious about frontier AI, being somewhere else feels like you're missing the conversation. That loop is very hard to break, at least for now.

r001.rationale: The response says San Francisco has an unusually high concentration of people with experience training and deploying large models, and identifies that talent density as a reason new labs start there.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it comes down to density, honestly. In the Bay Area, the people who can actually build these systems are concentrated within a few miles of each other. If you want to start a lab, you need maybe a dozen researchers who have real experience training large models, and those people are here. They came through Google, Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic, the universities, and they talk to each other constantly. You can bump into someone at a coffee shop and have a conversation that changes your research direction.

The second thing is capital. The investors who are willing to write very large checks for something that may not have revenue for years are mostly here, and they understand the field well enough to move quickly. That matters a lot when compute is so expensive. A new lab is not just a few laptops anymore; you need GPUs, and someone has to fund that early.

And then there is this feedback loop. Every new lab attracts more talent, more talent attracts more funding, and that pulls in the next wave of founders. People who left a big company to start something want to stay close to their former colleagues, their friends, their potential hires. So even though in principle you could do this research anywhere with an internet connection, in practice the social network is extremely local. Ideas move faster through conversations than through papers.

I would also say the culture tolerates failure in a way that is unusual. If your lab doesn't work out, you go join another one or start again. That lowers the cost of trying, so more people try.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the Bay Area has a concentrated pool of experienced AI researchers and identifies that talent density as a reason new labs start there.

astra-6.text:
I think a big part of it is the density of people working on AI. When you’re starting a lab, you need researchers, engineers, funding, and people who might use what you build. In San Francisco, those networks are close together, so it’s easier to find collaborators and get something started.

There’s also a feedback loop. People come because other people are already there. You meet someone, exchange ideas, and realize you want to work on the same problem. That can turn into a new team. Even though we can collaborate remotely, those informal interactions still matter, especially when the field is moving quickly.

r001.rationale: The candidate says San Francisco has a high density of people working on AI, making it easier for labs to find researchers and engineers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a big part of it is the density of people. If you’re starting an AI lab, you need researchers, engineers, funding, and people willing to try something uncertain. In San Francisco, those networks overlap, so it’s easier to meet a cofounder, recruit a team, or find someone who can help you think through an idea.

There’s also a feedback loop. When several labs are doing interesting work nearby, more people want to move there, and that makes it easier for the next lab to get started. You can exchange ideas over coffee, hear what problems other teams are running into, and get a sense of where the field is moving.

Of course, being there doesn’t guarantee good research. You still need your own judgment and the ability to focus. But that concentration of talent and opportunity makes it an attractive place to begin.

r001.rationale: The response says San Francisco has a density of researchers and engineers and that this concentration of talent makes it attractive to new AI labs.
